 16 November 2026, 3:26pm Teacher faces misconduct charge for ‘rough handling' of child while applying sunscreen
 Brianna McIlraith for NZ Herald Caption: The teacher told the tribunal she was focused on the tamariki being safe from the sun that day. Photo credit: RNZ It was a hot summer day in Christchurch and an early childhood educator needed to put sunscreen on her nursery class.
 When the final child to slip, slop and slap refused to do so, a teacher applied the sunscreen using force, so much so that the student was lifted from the ground and slipped before crawling away.
 The same teacher had told the centre's principal she needed a mental health day on another occasion as she was "about ready to throw children".
 The teacher, who has interim name suppression, was before the Teacher's Disciplinary Tribunal on Tuesday facing a charge of serious misconduct and/or misconduct after the 21 January 2025 incident.
 Tribunal chair Jamie O'Sullivan said this type of incident was often referred to as the "rough handling of children".
 The hearing was an opportunity for the teacher to speak to the tribunal.
 "I am extremely remorseful for what I've done," she said.
 "I'm hurt because teaching has been my passion ever since I was little."
 She told the tribunal she was focused on the tamariki being safe from the sun that day.
 It was not disclosed how old her students were, but they were in the nursery classroom.
 She was applying sunscreen to all her students before they could go outside to play.
 The final student was already outside playing and was refusing to get sunblock put on.
 "I wanted her to be safe at that point," the teacher said.
 The tribunal understood that at some point the child ended up with one arm and leg off the ground while the teacher struggled to apply the sunblock.
 When questioned by O'Sullivan about why the child was off the ground or picked up during the application, the teacher said she had sunblock-covered hands and, as she tried to apply it to the child, she kept moving away.
 She attempted to pick the child up under the armpits but, as her hands were slippery, they slipped down the child's arms so she was dangling by her wrists.
 The child crawled away to another educator. The tribunal did not disclose if the child was hurt.
 The teacher told the tribunal that in hindsight she should have given the child more space and time to put sunscreen on as there was no rush.
 "I basically took her right away to choose and I have learnt now the child has respect and autonomy over their own body and that wasn't my right to take that away from her."
 She told the tribunal that at the time of the incident, despite being provisionally registered, she was the longest-serving teacher at the centre, having worked there in some capacity for five years.
 Her mentor had previously left the job, and the centre had a high turnover, leaving her feeling alone.
 "I felt quite abandoned."
 'I had a feeling I wanted to throw a child'
 The tribunal heard she also took a mental health day after she developed feelings that she could "throw a child".
 She said she made that comment at work after she had found out a family member had died.
 She was outside with a child new to the centre and struggling to settle.
 The teacher was trying to console the child during nap time as she was waking other students. It was then she felt like she could harm the child.
 "I had a feeling I wanted to throw a child.
 "It wasn't that I harmed a child, it was a feeling that came to me."
 She removed herself from the room and told a colleague she was struggling. She took a mental health day and was told she could not return to the centre without a medical certificate.
 She also underwent a mental health assessment and counselling.
 She said if she were to return to teaching she would consider teaching an older age group as she'd be able to better communicate with them.
 "There's nothing really I can say, change or do to correct what I've done.
 "I can only improve myself."
 The tribunal will release its decision and any potential penalties at a later date.
 * This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald .
